## Exercises 1, 3, 4, 5 {#Exercises_Dates}

### Exercise 1 {-}

Convert the following to date or date/time objects.

**a)** September 13, 2010.

```{r}
mdy('September 13, 2010')
```


**b)** Sept 13, 2010.

```{r}
# mdy('Sept 13 2010')

```
This date fails, as the function does not recogonize September with the t ending the abbreviation. On the other hand, September (unabbriviated) is recognized. 

**c)** Sep 13, 2010.

```{r}
mdy('Sep 13, 2010')
```

**d)** S 13, 2010. Comment on the month abbreviation needs.

```{r}
#mdy('S 13, 2010')
```

The mdy function cannot recognize September from just the 'S', just as J could be either June or July. It is too abbreviated, where the correct would be Sep. 

**e)** 07-Dec-1941.

```{r}
dmy('07-Dec-1941')
```


**f)** 1-5-1998. Comment on why you might be wrong.

```{r}
dmy('1-5-1998')
mdy('1-5-1998')

```

We do not know if the order goes month-day-year or day-month-year, because 1-5 could be January 5th, or May 1st, which is a significant difference. 

**g)** 21-5-1998. Comment on why you know you are correct.

```{r}
dmy('21-5-1998')
```

We know this date goes D-M-Y, because there are not 21 months in the year. 

**h)** 2020-May-5 10:30 am

```{r}
ymd_hm('2020-May-5 10:30 am')
```

We do not specify the timezone, so the function assumes UTC as the standard. 

**i)** 2020-May-5 10:30 am PDT (ex Seattle)

```{r}
ymd_hm('2020-May-5 10:30 am', tz = 'US/Pacific')
```

In looking at the provided wiki link of timezones, you can find the PDT locations. PDT and PT are not recognized, but they use the identifier 'US/Pacific' since you are looking specifically at pacific time. 

**j)** 2020-May-5 10:30 am AST (ex Puerto Rico)

```{r}
ymd_hm('2020-May-5 10:30 am', tz = 'America/Puerto_Rico')
```

For Atlantic Standard time, we can use the identifier 'America/Puerto_Rico', as this is common island time in the carribean and similar vacation paradises. 

### Exercise 3 {-}

Suppose you have arranged for a phone call to be at 3 pm on May 8, 2025 at Arizona time. However, the recipient will be in Auckland, NZ. What time will it be there? 

```{r}
mdy_hm('05-08-2025 15:00', tz = "US/Arizona")
call.time <- mdy_hm('May 8, 2025 3:00 PM', tz = "US/Arizona")
#these produce the same output


with_tz(call.time, 'NZ/Auckland')
```

**Conclusion:** If my bestie is in New Zeleand and I know he has a bedtime of 10:00 pm, I should probably call before 3 pm AZ time to not disrupt his slumber. 

### Exercise 4 {-}

From this book's [GitHub](https://github.com/BuscagliaR/STA_444_v2/) directory, navigate to the `data-raw` directory and then download the `Pulliam_Airport_Weather_Station.csv` data file. (*There are several weather station files. Make sure you get the correct one!*)  There is a `DATE` column (is it of type `date` when you import the data?) as well as the Maximum and Minimum temperature. For the last 5 years of data included in the file, plot the time series of daily maximum temperature with date on the x-axis. Write your code so that it will work if I update the date set. *Hint: Find the maximum date in the data set and then subtract 5 years. Will there be a difference if you use `dyears(5)` vs `years(5)`? Which seems more appropriate here?*


```{r}
Pulliam_Airport_Weather_Station <- read.csv("../data-raw/Pulliam_Airport_Weather_Station.csv")

cleaned.ap.weather <- Pulliam_Airport_Weather_Station %>%
  select(DATE, TMIN, TMAX)

recent <- max(cleaned.ap.weather$DATE) #Max date is sept 15, 2019 and returns as a string
yrs.ago5 <- ymd(recent) - dyears(5) #dyears provides a timestamp, which includes duration, years only display the period. 


last.5.yrs <- cleaned.ap.weather %>%
  filter(ymd(DATE) > yrs.ago5)

ggplot(last.5.yrs, aes(x = DATE, y = TMAX, colour = month(DATE, label = TRUE))) +
  geom_jitter() +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Max Temperature", title = "Pulliam Airport Temps")
#month color added for pizzaz
```

### Exercise 5 {-}

It turns out there is some interesting periodicity regarding the number of births on particular days of the year.

**a)** Using the `mosaicData` package, load the data set `Births78` which records the number of children born on each day in the United States in 1978. Because this problem is intended to show how to calculate the information using the `date`, remove all the columns *except* `date` and `births`.

```{r}
library("mosaicData")
data("Births78")

cleaned.birth <- Births78 %>%
  select(date, births)
```


**b)** Graph the number of `births` vs the `date` with date on the x-axis. What stands out to you? Why do you think we have this trend?

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(cleaned.birth, aes(x = date, y = births)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth()

```

**Conclusion:** We see 2 notable trends as 2 seperate waves. This seems like there may be some discrepency in the data, due to the vertical uniformity in the graph. I wonder if the lower bound was recorded at the beginning of the day, where as the upper bound was at the end of the day. 


**c)** To test your assumption, we need to figure out the what day of the week each observation is. Use `dplyr::mutate` to add a new column named `dow` that is the day of the week (Monday, Tuesday, etc). This calculation will involve some function in the `lubridate` package and the `date` column.

```{r}
library(lubridate)

mutated.births <- cleaned.birth %>%
  mutate(dow = wday(date, label = TRUE)) #sunday = 1, sat = 7
```


**d)** Plot the data with the point color being determined by the day of the week variable.

```{r}

ggplot(mutated.births, aes(x = date, y = births, color = dow)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Babies Born in 1978",
  subtitle = "Colored by Day of Week")


```

**Conclusion:** By faceting by color, we can see a pattern of more babies being born Monday - Friday, and less on the weekends. This could suggest the babies want to sleep in on the weekend, thus remaining in utero.
